paper_title: Spectral Gaps with Quantum Counting Queries and Oblivious State Preparation
statement: 5 A lower bound in the Black-Box model In this section we derive a lower bound for the problem of deciding the existence of a spectral gap of a binary matrix, in the so-called Black-Box access model. Here we assume a unitary OA through which we can query elements of the matrix A via: OA : |i⟩ |j⟩ |0⟩ 7→ |i⟩ |j⟩ |Ai,j ⟩ . Several lower bounds are known for related problems. A straightforward query lower bound for determining the midpoint µk can be obtained from the median problem [68]. Let A be a quantum algorithm which, given OA , and an integer k, it returns any (classical) ek such that µ ek ∈ (λk , λk+1 ). Then A can be directly used to solve the median value µ problem, where, given oracle access to a sequence of N numbers {x1 , . . . , xN }, where N is even, we seek to find a number that lies strictly inside x ∈ (xN/2 , xN/2 + 1). Such a sequence can be seen as the elements of a diagonal matrix, and the eigenvalues of such a matrix are the diagonal elements themselves. [68] proved a Ω(N ) query lower bound for the median problem, assuming that we have oracle access to a quantum circuit implementing ek is inside the sequence. Indeed, the same bound holds even if we only want to verify that µ the correct interval, since this generalizes the counting problem [68, 69, 70]. Here we obtain a stronger lower bound for deciding whether there exists a gap between two consecutive eigenvalues, inspired by the reductions of [56, 57]. We remark that the construction below is inherently non-Hermitian. Whether analogous black-box lower bounds hold for Hermitian matrices remains an open question.

Given a matrix A ∈ {0, 1}N ×N , a unitary OA : |i⟩ |j⟩ |0⟩ 7→ |i⟩ |j⟩ |Ai,j ⟩, and an integer k, any quantum algorithm which answers TRUE if ∆k := |λk (A) − λk+1 (A)| > 0, and FALSE otherwise, must execute Ω(N 2 ) queries to OA . Here the eigenvalues of A are order such that Re(λ1 ) ≥ Re(λ2 ) ≥ . . . ≥ Re(λN ), and if Re(λk ) = Re(λk+1 ), then Im(λk ) ≥ Im(λk+1 ). Proof. The proof closely follows the techniques of [56, 57] for other similar problems (rank, determinant, matrix power, and inverse), essentially by reducing the problem to counting 2 the number of triangles in a directed graph. Assume that we are given a set X ∈ {0, 1}N P 2 and the value a = ⌈N 2 /2⌉, and we ask whether N i=1 Xi = a. The query complexity of this problem is Ω(N 2 ) [56]. For the reduction the first step is to create a couple of graphs. We create a bipartite graph G, with N sources si and N targets tj , and we insert an edge between si and tj iff XiN +j = 1. We also create a utility node v, which has N outgoing edges to every one of the sources, and N incoming edges from every one of the targets. Thereafter, we construct a second bipartite graph G′ which also has N sources s′i , N targets t′j , and a utility node v ′ . We create exactly a edges between the sources and the targets, in a round-robin manner, so that the edges are “evenly distributed” among the two vertex sets (for each si , we add roughly ⌈a/N ⌉ outgoing edges). Finally, we add N edges from v ′ to every s′i , and N edges from every t′j to v ′ . Note that the two graphs are disjoint. Consider the larger graph F = (V ∪ V ′ , E ∪ E ′ ), and its adjacency matrix A. F has 4N + 2 nodes.
